title: On the Origin of Beyond-Classical Advantage in the Parity-Permutation Problem
authors: Jayashree Karmakar, Biswadeep Chatterjee, Rafiuddin Gazi, Ananya Chakraborty, Snehasish Roy Chowdhury, Manik Banik, Tamal Guha, Sahil Gopalkrishna Naik, Kunika Agarwal
abstract: We investigate the task of identifying the parity (odd vs even) of an unknown permutation applied to $n$ particles. Classically, using fewer than $n$ distinct labels per particle limits the success probability to random guessing, whereas quantum mechanics, exploiting entanglement in both preparation and measurement, accomplishes the task perfectly with as few as $\big\lceil \sqrt{n}\big\rceil$ levels per particle [\href{https://doi.org/10.1103/yhyv-xnwq}{PRL {\bf 135}, 260603 (2025)}]. We show that even without entangled preparation, quantum theory still offers a probabilistic advantage over classical strategies. Moreover, such product preparations yield perfect success in locally quantum theories, where elementary systems are quantum but their composition follows the minimal tensor product structure of generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs). We further identify GPT models that accomplish the task with certainty without requiring entanglement either at the preparation stage or at the measurement stage. Our central result establishes that the linear dimension of the elementary systems, rather than entanglement, is the fundamental resource governing the existence of probabilistic advantage in the permutation parity problem. In particular, below the required dimension threshold, no amount of entanglement can improve upon the random-guessing limit.
summary: The paper analyzes the Parity-Permutation Problem to pinpoint the fundamental resource enabling quantum advantage. It proves that this advantage depends not on entanglement itself, but on the linear dimension of the underlying state space ($L_{dS} \geq n$). This result is significant because it provides a necessary and sufficient condition for detecting non-classical correlations using simple product-state preparations.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental resource governing quantum advantage when solving the Parity-Permutation Problem, $P[n]$. It seeks to determine if entanglement or merely the linear dimension of the state space is responsible for non-classical success probabilities.
main_result: The existence of a probabilistic advantage in $P[n]$ is fundamentally characterized by the linear dimension ($L_{dS}$) of the underlying theory, requiring $L_{dS} \geq n$. This advantage can be achieved using product-state preparations, suggesting that entanglement is not strictly necessary for an operational gain.
method: The analysis uses information theoretic tools applied to Generalized Probabilistic Theories (GPTs) to distinguish between two mixed states ($\chi_E$ and $\chi_O$) corresponding to even and odd permutations. Success probabilities are calculated using bounds like the Helstrom bound.
model_or_system: The problem is modeled as determining the parity of a permutation applied to $n$ particles, analyzed first with qubits ($P[3]$) and then generalized to abstract GPTs characterized by their linear dimension $L_{dS}$.
key_observables: Success probability ($P[n]$), Linear Dimension ($L_{dS}$), Operational Dimension (OD).
important_parameters: The number of particles, $n$; the required minimum local dimension for advantage; $\lceil\sqrt{n}ceil$ levels.
main_assumptions: The work explores moving beyond standard quantum mechanics by analyzing locally quantum theories and GPTs to test the necessity of entanglement.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates optimal product state preparation achieving $7/8$ success for $P[3]$, and also shows an alternative scenario achieving perfect success without entanglement. Table II details measurement settings used to distinguish states.
paper_structure: The paper establishes classical limits, demonstrates quantum advantage using qubits ($P[3]$), then analyzes optimal product vs. bi-separable preparations, culminating in a general theorem characterizing the necessary condition for advantage based on the linear dimension within GPTs.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep theoretical characterization of resource theories, showing that operational advantages can be witnessed by simple dimensional constraints rather than requiring complex entanglement structures, which is highly relevant for understanding physical limits in quantum information processing.
